title: CallMap: test every way a call can go

steps.text: Teams that build voice agents test them on simulated calls. Before every launch, and after every prompt change.
Here's the problem. A test suite can pass every test, and still miss the calls that matter.
Most generated tests follow the easy path: a caller who answers clearly, in order, the first time.
Real callers don't. They change an answer, ask too early, or push back. That's where agents break.
And no one can say which of those calls were never tested. Counting tests doesn't tell you.
{{product}} maps every way a call can go, tests each one, and shows you what was never tested.
It works in four steps. It maps the call, writes tests aimed at the map, runs them as simulated calls, and closes the gaps.
Step one: map the call.
Here's an example: a pharmacy's refill agent. It starts from the requirements the team already wrote.
It turns them into a map. Every decision the agent makes, every answer a caller can give, and every way a caller can break the order.
Each path gets checks, and a priority. High risk means a mistake could hurt someone, like a missed side effect.
Step two: write tests aimed at the map.
First, it measures the team's current suite. Fifty tests, all passing. But they cover thirty-one percent of the map.
Not one test has a caller who changes an answer later.
So it writes tests for the gaps. Each one says exactly what the caller says, and when.
Tests that repeat a covered path are dropped. Seventy-two tests now cover ninety-five percent.
Step three: run each test as a simulated call.
It runs every test as a call, and checks the agent against the map.
Here's one that failed.
Thanks, Mr. Ortiz. Any new side effects since your last refill?
No, nothing.
Great. Would you like pickup or delivery?
Pickup. Oh, actually, I've been dizzy since my dose went up.
Okay. Your refill will be ready Thursday after two p.m.
The caller mentioned dizziness after the side-effect question, and the agent just booked the pickup. It should have sent him to a pharmacist. The old suite never had this call.
Step four: close the gaps.
Some paths can't be tested yet, because the requirements don't say what the agent should do. Is a refill on day twenty-three too early? It asks the pharmacist, instead of guessing.
And every prompt change runs again. The team sees coverage and failures together, so a fix never quietly breaks another path.
Passing tests show what worked. {{product}} shows what was never tested.
